title: Best Engine wit claude code?
author: NoAssociation1032
selftext: ive only been using UE5, but im seeing some stuff on instagram of people using godot and it looks INSANELY polished, idk if they just buy assets and let it write logic, for me it does both lol it creates assets in blender then does logic in UE5 but its a pain in the ass cuz i gotta keep telling it to fix bugs, and it takes time, like lots of time, so im wondering is Godot better? or even unity? after all it comes down to the engine's exposed API or MCP right?

replies.author: Mother-Hedgehog-5628
replies.body:
This, most of the stuff you will see is just clickbait or lots and lots of effort has been put in to get there. 

Unreal has tons of stuff too that you should be using but you need to do some research... between GASP, Metahuman, Mutable and Procedural Content Generation.... unreal has nearly all the bones you need to make a game look tripple A - it just takes some time to learn all the parts - modern unreal has been built around the idea of having frameworks ready to go for games so you dont need to reinvent the wheel.

replies.body: hows the quality tho? i mean no lumen and nanite, thats ok?

replies.author: BinniesPurp
replies.body:
If you arnt sure what lumen and nanite do you won't benifit from it 

You need a built out PBR system with global scene illumination for lumen, and you need to already be able to view on the profiler that you're wasting draw calls on the GPU before you get any fps increase from nanite

Unless you design your scene and your mesh topology around nanite itself, you'll often lose fps, not gain fps

comments.author: Hakim3i
comments.body:
I've tested all three engines with Claude Code on fairly large projects.

**Godot is the best so far**, mainly because it's lightweight and AI can work with it much faster. Even graphically, it's not bad at all and can deliver results on par with Unity, depending on the project.

**Unity is the best middle ground** if your game needs a balance between graphics, performance, flexibility, and development speed.

**Unreal Engine is honestly the worst experience when it comes to AI-assisted development.** Everything takes longer, debugging can be painful, and it tends to consume a lot more tokens just to get things working. Don't get me wrong, the visual results can be amazing, but the development workflow is much heavier.

Another thing to consider is your hardware. If you're running something like 16GB of RAM and an RTX 5060, Unreal development and testing can become a huge bottleneck, especially on larger projects, I have 32GB of RAM and RTX 5070TI and still found out it is slow on Unreal.
